title: Multiscale deformation and failure mechanisms of expansive soils
subtitle: Multiscale geotechnical mechanics
shortTitle: Multiscale deformation and failure mechanisms of expansive soils
summary: Swelling–shrinkage deformation and slope instability in expansive soils are closely related to moisture changes, whose effects involve mineral interlayer structures, soil fracture propagation, and slope deformation. This study uses molecular dynamics simulations of montmorillonite, CCNBD fracture propagation tests, and fractured-slope model tests to investigate changes in interlayer structure, fracture-tip deformation, and slope strain evolution, respectively. The results show that hydration history affects the interlayer structure of montmorillonite, water ingress into fractures alters strain propagation and fracture resistance, and pre-existing fractures and infiltration jointly influence slope deformation and shallow sliding.

blocks.text: Swelling–shrinkage deformation and slope instability in expansive soils are closely related to moisture changes, whose effects involve mineral interlayer structures, soil fracture propagation, and slope deformation. This study uses molecular dynamics simulations of montmorillonite, CCNBD fracture propagation tests, and fractured-slope model tests to investigate changes in interlayer structure, fracture-tip deformation, and slope strain evolution, respectively. The results show that hydration history affects the interlayer structure of montmorillonite, water ingress into fractures alters strain propagation and fracture resistance, and pre-existing fractures and infiltration jointly influence slope deformation and shallow sliding.

media.alt: Molecular models of Na- and Ca-montmorillonite
media.label: Figure 1 Molecular models of Na- and Ca-montmorillonite
media.caption: Successive hydration and dehydration steps inherit the equilibrated configuration from the preceding state, allowing interlayer structures formed by different histories to be compared at the same interlayer water content.

media.label: Figure 2 CCNBD fracture propagation test system
media.caption: The loading system, digital image correlation, and electrical resistance measurements synchronously record load, surface strain, and resistance changes to track fracture propagation and the evolution of internal damage.

media.label: Figure 3 Design of fractured-slope model tests
media.caption: After specimen preparation, speckles are applied and slope models with different fracture configurations are assembled for loading or infiltration tests. VIC-2d is used to analyze strain on the slope surface.

media.alt: Basal spacing and path differences during hydration and dehydration
media.label: Figure 4 Basal spacing and path differences during hydration and dehydration
media.caption: Δd001 is the mean spacing during hydration minus the mean spacing during dehydration at the same interlayer water content. The separation between hydration and dehydration paths for Na- and Ca-montmorillonite varies with hydration state, and the mean spacings are similar at some states.

media.alt: Load and strain evolution during Mode I tensile failure
media.label: Figure 5 Load and strain evolution during Mode I tensile failure
media.caption: Load, the resistivity-based damage variable Dρ, and tensile strain measured by digital image correlation jointly record fracture propagation. A strain concentration zone forms before peak load, and the crack propagates rapidly from the tip after the peak.

media.alt: Load and strain evolution during Mode II shear failure
media.label: Figure 6 Load and strain evolution during Mode II shear failure
media.caption: Shear strain develops from the loading region toward the fracture tip, and strain zones expand and coalesce near peak load. The damage variable provides an additional record of the failure process.

media.alt: Strain evolution in slope models under water injection
media.label: Figure 7 Strain evolution in slope models under water injection
media.caption: Four panels compare strain distributions in single-fracture models with fracture angles of 10° and 20° under two loading levels. Under the combined effects of loading and water injection, strain develops along the fractures and within localized parts of the slope. Each panel uses an independent color scale.

blocks.text: At the microscopic scale, path-dependent differences in water-molecule distribution and cation hydration sustain hysteresis in the interlayer structure of montmorillonite. At the specimen scale, water ingress into fractures causes localized softening and alters crack propagation. At the slope scale, pre-existing fractures affect strain transfer, loading promotes sliding along fracture interfaces, and infiltration promotes the formation of shallow slip surfaces. The model tests indicate that the middle and toe of the slope warrant particular attention in reinforcement.

media.alt: Mechanistic links between interlayer structure and local hydration
media.label: Figure 8 Mechanistic links between interlayer structure and local hydration
media.caption: Path-dependent differences in water-molecule occupancy, cation hydration, and interactions jointly maintain differences in interlayer structure and provide mechanistic clues for understanding differential swelling and shrinkage at higher scales.

media.alt: Strain distributions with and without water injection into fractures
media.label: Figure 9 Strain distributions with and without water injection into fractures
media.caption: Comparisons between specimens show that, without water injection, strain develops mainly from the loading end toward the fracture; with water injection, softened regions around the fracture also contribute to deformation. The figure compares spatial distributions under different water-ingress conditions.
